_comment: A synthetic 12-week interval for the demo, written against the existing
demo consultation (fixtures/demo_consultation.summary.json) so it is the
same patient, the same five commitments, and the same 'very low dose' gap.
The point of this file is that the brief must be MADE OF interval data. A
brief assembled from one two-week check-in where everything went fine is a
summary with extra steps. So this interval is deliberately mixed: the
tablet gets collected late, the dose gap is closed by a pharmacy label that
disagrees with what the patient remembers being told, adherence slips in
the middle weeks for an ordinary reason, the blood test silently does not
happen, and one over-replacement symptom appears at week 9 and a second at
week 11 — which is the cluster the whole product exists to catch, assembled
one call at a time exactly as it would be in life.
Nothing here is a clinical judgement. Every entry is something a patient
said or a date that passed. The interpretation stays where it belongs: with
the doctor reading the brief.

_comment: How the medication row should stand at the END of the interval, after
every call below has been applied. The seed command replays the calls in
order rather than writing this directly — this block is here so the
expected end state is reviewable in one place.
The dosage is the interesting field: the consultation said 'very low
dose', which is authoritative and unusable at the same time. The label
closes it, and the label disagrees with what the patient remembers. That
disagreement is recorded as a note for the patient to raise, not resolved
— it is not Cadence's place to decide which is right.

expected_end_state._source_note: Only the dosage is label-sourced, because only the dosage was a gap. The clinician stated a name and a frequency, so the label does not overwrite either — it records the disagreement as a note and leaves the clinician's words standing. Three notes result, and each is a real thing worth raising at the next appointment.
expected_end_state.name: thyroid replacement medication
expected_end_state.frequency: every day, ideally around the same time each day
expected_end_state._adherence_note: A snapshot, not a history: they missed three or four doses around week 4 and were back on it by week 9, so the field reads every_day. The missed fortnight is not lost — it is an event, dated to when it happened rather than to the call that surfaced it. A brief that read this field alone would miss it, which is why the chronology exists.
notes: The label says name is "levothyroxine"; your clinician said "thyroid replacement medication". Worth checking with them which to follow.
The label says frequency is "one tablet each morning"; your clinician said "every day, ideally around the same time each day". Worth checking with them which to follow.

check_ins._comment: Day 1. The first-contact call: not a check-in, an orientation. Nothing has happened yet and nothing should be graded.
check_ins.transcript: Hi Sam, it's Cadence — just a quick one the day after your appointment. // Oh, hello. Yes. // I wanted to check you've got what you need to get started. Has the prescription come through yet? // Not yet, no. He said he'd send it and I could pick it up next time I'm at the clinic, but I'm not back there for a bit. // That's fine, I'll ask again in a few days. And when you do start it, do you know what time of day suits you? // Not really. Mornings are a write-off for me, honestly. // Understood — I'll leave that until you've actually got the tablets in hand.

outcomes.patient_words: Not yet, no. He said he'd send it and I could pick it up next time I'm at the clinic

check_ins._comment: Week 2. Collected, but nine days late, and the dose gap is still open. The label photo is what closes it — and the label disagrees with the patient's memory.
check_ins.transcript: Hi Sam. Did you manage to pick up the prescription? // I did, yeah, finally. I was at the clinic on Tuesday so I got it then. // Good. Have you taken the first one? // I took one that evening, yes. // I've got a note here that the dose wasn't written down clearly at the appointment. Would you be able to read me what the label says? // It says levothyroxine, 25 micrograms, one tablet each morning. // Thank you — so that's levothyroxine, 25 micrograms, one each morning. Is that right? // That's what it says, yeah. Though I thought he said it was a very low dose, he didn't say a number. // I'll record both — worth asking him which to follow. And what time works for taking it? // Half two in the afternoon, if I'm honest. That's when I'm properly awake. // Then half two it is.

_comment: Week 9. The first over-replacement symptom. It is mentioned in passing,
it sounds like nothing, and the patient does not connect it to the
tablet — which is precisely why a fixed script never finds it. One
symptom is not a cluster; nothing fires yet, and nothing should.
check_ins.transcript: Hi Sam. How have things been? // Not bad. Bit better than I was. // How tired, one to ten? // Five, I'd say. // That's come down. Anything new at all, even things that seem unrelated? // Not really. I've been sleeping badly, but that's just me. // Badly how? // Awake at three, four in the morning. Every night for a couple of weeks now. Nothing to do with the thyroid, I shouldn't think. // I'll make a note of it either way. And the blood test — has that been booked? // No. Nobody's contacted me about it.

_comment: Week 11. The second symptom lands and the cluster assembles — across
calls two weeks apart, which is exactly why the counting is Python's
job and not the model's. The agent reads the red flag's patient-facing
line verbatim; it does not compose a warning and does not say the word
dose.
The blood test is now overdue. Note that nobody failed at anything
here: it was ordered, and it silently did not happen. That is the
single most useful line in the brief.
check_ins.transcript: Hi Sam. How have you been? // Alright. Warm, mostly. // Warm? // I've been really hot. Sat in the garden in a t-shirt last week and everyone else had coats on. Sister said I'd gone mad. // How long has that been going on? // Two weeks, about. // And the sleeping? // Still bad. Still up at three. // Thank you for telling me. I want to read you something exactly as it's written for your condition, because two of the things you've described are on it. [red flag patient-facing line read verbatim] // Right. Should I stop taking it? // That's not something I can advise on — that's a question for your clinician, and it's worth contacting them about this. I'll make sure it's all written down for them. // Okay. // And the tiredness, one to ten? // Four. // Has the blood test happened? // No. Still nothing.

_comment: The second consultation — scheduled, not yet happened. It is deliberately
empty of a transcript and a summary, because it has none: the appointment
is four days away.
This is the visit the brief is FOR. Without a row here the brief is an
artifact with no destination, and the demo's fourth beat — the patient
walks in and hands the doctor this — has nothing on the calendar to walk
into. With it, the interval has two ends: a consultation twelve weeks
behind and an appointment four days ahead, and everything above sits
between them.
It is NOT a completed visit. A seeded Visit 2 with its own summary would
turn the brief into history — a record of an appointment that already
went well — when the whole claim is that the brief changes how the next
appointment starts. The arrow points forward, so the data must too.
previous_brief_id is set by the seed command to the brief it generates,
which is the return arrow the schema added for exactly this: a visit the
patient did not walk into cold.
Not the brief itself — the brief is generated. This is what the interval
above should make available to it, kept here so a generated brief can be
checked against what actually happened rather than read for plausibility.
Every line is a fact from a call or a date that passed.
